Can living in a house make someone the owner?

Only if they meet every element of the adverse possession statute for ten years, including a written document that looks like a title and payment of the property taxes. Section 37-1-22 NMSA 1978 controls. Someone who moves into a vacant house with no paper claim and never pays the tax bill is nowhere close.

The statute requires adverse possession "continuously and in good faith under color of title for ten years," with no lawsuit brought by the true owner in that time. Once those conditions are met, the occupant may keep the land described in the writing that gives color of title, and an owner who sat on a claim for the ten years is barred. Adverse possession is defined as "an actual and visible appropriation of land, commenced and continued under a color of title and claim of right inconsistent with and hostile to the claim of another."

A separate tax condition closes the statute. Adverse possession isn't established unless the claimant, or those the claimant takes through, continuously paid all state, county and municipal taxes assessed against the property during the ten years.

Elements a claimant must prove

Legal aid guidance prepared for the state's Land Grant Council groups the requirements in three parts: open, continuous, exclusive, actual, visible, hostile and notorious possession for ten years, color of title, and payment of taxes. Every one must hold for the full ten years, and failing any one defeats the claim.

  • Continuous: possession can't be on and off.
  • Actual: the claimant must physically enter. Holding a deed isn't enough, because the ten years don't begin until the claimant enters and takes possession.
  • Open and notorious: the claimant can't hide. The clock doesn't run until the possession is visible enough to give the owner notice.
  • Exclusive: possession can't be shared with the public or other users. If others try to use the land, the claimant has to keep them out.
  • Hostile: the occupant must be there without any right or permission, so the possession is plainly against the owner's rights.
Requirements at a glance
RequirementWhat the claimant needs
TimeTen years, with no suit by the owner
Written claimColor of title, held in good faith
TaxesAll state, county and municipal taxes paid continuously
ProofClear and convincing evidence

The claimant carries the burden. Adverse possession must be proved by clear and convincing evidence, and it can't be established by inference or implication.

Color of title

Color of title is a written document that purports to give the occupant title, even if it turns out to be defective. New Mexico courts have accepted quitclaim deeds, a certificate of sale for taxes, a government patent, a void deed, and a quiet title decree or other court judgment.

Case notes under 37-1-22 add detail. A recorded quitclaim deed, executed and acknowledged one day and recorded the next, with the buyer taking immediate possession, established color of title in one case. A tax deed can serve even when void for lack of title in the grantor, but not if its land description is too weak to identify the property. In one case involving siblings who owned together, a deed to one sibling and his wife did not establish color of title.

A stray deed in the record can matter. If someone lives in your house and has recorded a deed, even a weak one, the ten-year clock may have started. Our New Mexico quitclaim deed guide explains the form that often shows up in these disputes.

Tenants and guests

Almost never, because permission defeats hostility. Where the original entry was permissive, the statute of limitations doesn't begin to run until an adverse holding is declared and notice of the change reaches the owner. Mere possession isn't enough. Possession that starts as a tenancy is presumed permissive, and ending that presumption takes proof, or a presumption, that the owner was told the occupant now claims against them.

Someone who enters a vacant house without permission is in a different position, but the extra requirements still apply. Claimants have won by marking boundaries, posting no-trespassing signs, clearing land, fencing, limiting access and paying taxes. Together, those facts gave the owner notice. Simply staying in a house with none of those steps is thin evidence.

The statute also protects some owners with a disability. If the person entitled to sue was imprisoned, of unsound mind or under the age of majority when the cause of action first accrued, they get one year after the disability ends to bring suit. Cumulative disabilities don't extend the bar.

Government land, water rights and land grants

Not every kind of property can be taken this way. Adverse possession usually can't be applied against governmental property, only private property. Land grants governed as political subdivisions were made immune from adverse possession claims in 2007 under 49-1-11.2, except for claims that had already vested by June 15, 2007.

Two more limits apply. New Mexico's water code means water rights can't be obtained through adverse possession, and the state's rights in highways can't be divested by it under a cross-referenced statute.

How an owner removes someone with no right to be there

Through a court case. A landlord must go to court before evicting a tenant, and a person living in a home who isn't on the lease can't be evicted like a tenant. That person is removed through "forcible entry," using Form 4-203, Complaint in Forcible Entry. At the hearing, the judge decides whether the person must leave and how much time they have to move out.

Section 35-10-1 NMSA 1978 lists the grounds for a forcible entry or unlawful detainer action in magistrate court. The first applies directly to uninvited occupants: the defendant entered and occupied the land of another against the owner's will or consent and refused to vacate after notice from the owner, agent or attorney. The other grounds cover:

  • A tenant who holds over after the lease ends or contrary to its terms.
  • A tenant who fails to pay rent when due.
  • An occupant who stays after a mortgage foreclosure or execution sale, unless claiming title paramount to the mortgage or derived from the purchaser.
  • A month-to-month tenant or tenant at will who stays after thirty days' written notice to vacate.

The district court has concurrent jurisdiction when the rent or reasonable rental value is $50 or more per month. These actions are summary proceedings that settle nothing about title. A forcible entry case puts the parties back in their prior positions but doesn't decide who owns the house.

When trespassing is a crime

Section 30-14-1.1 NMSA 1978 makes several kinds of trespass a misdemeanor. One is entering and remaining on another's land after being asked to leave. Others are entering land posted against trespass at every roadway or apparent way of access, and driving a vehicle onto fenced land except through an apparent way of access.

The same section creates civil liability. A person who enters another's land without permission and damages the realty or its improvements, including buildings, structures, trees and shrubs, owes double the appraised value of the damage to the owner, lessee or person in lawful possession.

The offense turns on a request to leave, so keep a dated written request. Talk to an attorney before acting.

Protecting a vacant or inherited house

Keep the paper record clean and the taxes current. These steps follow from the statute:

  • Visit the property on a schedule, and document each visit with dates and photos.
  • Post no-trespassing signs and keep the property secured.
  • Pay the property tax yourself. A claimant who hasn't paid can't succeed, and a delinquency can lead to a tax sale, covered in our New Mexico tax deed guide.
  • Check the county clerk's records for any deed or affidavit recorded by someone else.
  • Give written notice to anyone staying without permission, and keep a copy.

Under a 1954 decision, the general rule is that continuity of adverse possession is interrupted if the land is forfeited to the state for taxes. That is one more reason to keep the tax record current.

Owners who inherited a house and can't manage an occupant, repairs or back taxes sometimes sell as is. Cash Home Buyers doesn't promise a price in advance. Anyone who buys will want to know who lives in the house and whether a court case is pending, so share that up front.

Frequently asked questions

How long does adverse possession take in New Mexico?

Ten years of continuous possession under color of title, in good faith, with all taxes paid, under 37-1-22 NMSA 1978. The claimant must prove it by clear and convincing evidence.

Do squatters have rights in New Mexico?

A person with no written claim to title who hasn't paid the property taxes can't meet the statute. The owner removes an occupant through a forcible entry complaint in court.

Do adverse possession claimants have to pay property taxes?

Yes. Adverse possession isn't established unless the claimant or predecessors continuously paid all state, county and municipal taxes assessed during the ten years.

How do I remove someone who is not on the lease?

File Form 4-203, Complaint in Forcible Entry. The judge decides whether the person must leave and sets the time to move out.

Is it a crime to stay on someone's land after being told to leave?

Yes. Section 30-14-1.1 makes it a misdemeanor to enter and remain on another's land after being asked to leave. A forcible entry case, by contrast, doesn't decide title, so a separate action is needed to settle ownership.

The law that covers rentals

The Uniform Owner-Resident Relations Act, Chapter 47, Article 8 of the New Mexico Statutes, sets the main rules for residential rentals. It calls landlords "owners" and tenants "residents," so a search for "New Mexico tenant rights" ends up under that wording.

The act covers deposits, entry, rent, late fees, notices and retaliation. If you own a rented house, a sale happens on top of those duties, and your showing schedule has to fit around the resident's rights.

Rules sellers run into most often
TopicRuleStatute section
Deposit, lease under one yearNo more than one month's rent47-8-18(A)(2)
Deposit refund or itemized listWithin thirty days of termination or departure, whichever is later47-8-18(C)
Bad faith deposit retention$250 civil penalty payable to the resident47-8-18(E)
Entry to inspect or show the unitTwenty-four hours written notice unless agreed otherwise47-8-24(A)
Late feeUp to five percent of rent per period, if the agreement provides for it47-8-15(D)
Rent increaseWritten notice at least thirty days before the rental date or the end of the term47-8-15(F)
Month-to-month terminationWritten notice at least thirty days before the rental date47-8-37(B)
Nonpayment of rentThree days after written notice47-8-33(D)

Security deposits

An owner may take a reasonable deposit to cover damage during the residency. For agreements shorter than one year, the deposit can't exceed one month's rent. Under an annual agreement, a deposit above one month's rent means the owner owes the resident interest each year.

The owner may apply the deposit to unpaid rent and to damage caused by the resident's noncompliance, but never to normal wear and tear. After that, the owner has thirty days to mail an itemized written list of deductions, plus any balance, to the resident's last known address.

Missing that deadline is costly. The owner forfeits the right to withhold any part of the deposit, to counterclaim in a suit over it and to bring a separate action for damage to the property. Court costs and reasonable attorney fees can be added. A 2025 Court of Appeals decision confirmed that the forfeiture applies when the owner fails to itemize, and that a timely itemization keeps a later damage claim alive.

The thirty-day clock matters most if a tenant moves out around closing. It runs from the later of termination or departure, so the sale contract should name who handles the itemization.

Can a landlord show the house to buyers?

Yes, with notice. Section 47-8-24 lets an owner enter a dwelling to exhibit it to prospective or actual purchasers, and also for inspections, repairs and visits from mortgagees or contractors.

Unless the owner and resident agree otherwise, the owner must first give twenty-four hours written notice stating the intent to enter, the purpose, the date and a reasonable estimate of the time frame. Entry without consent is allowed in an emergency. The notice rule also doesn't apply to repairs within seven days of a resident's request or to entry with a public official or a utility representative.

  • If the resident offers reasonable alternate dates, the owner must try to accommodate them when practicable and not economically harmful.
  • The owner may not abuse the right of access.
  • If the resident refuses lawful access, the owner can seek an injunction to compel access or terminate the agreement, and can recover damages.
  • If the owner enters unlawfully or makes repeated demands that interfere with quiet enjoyment, the resident can seek an injunction or terminate the agreement and recover damages.

A rented house is slower to show than a vacant one. Every open house or buyer walkthrough needs its own written notice.

Rent, late fees and increases

Rent is due when the agreement says, and a late fee is allowed only if the agreement provides for one. A 2025 amendment effective June 20, 2025 cut the cap on late fees from ten percent to five percent of rent per rental period.

Late fees can be figured only on rent. Deposits, additional fees and utilities are left out of the calculation. To charge the fee, the owner must give notice of it no later than the last day of the next rental period after the default. An older Court of Appeals case denied late fees to landlords who skipped that notice.

For a month-to-month residency, rent can go up by written notice at least thirty days before the periodic rental date. For a fixed term, the notice must come at least thirty days before the term ends. Unless both sides agree in writing, rent paid can't be allocated to deposits or damages.

Ending a tenancy or evicting for nonpayment

Notices in New Mexico are short and must follow the statute exactly. For nonpayment, the resident has three days after written notice of nonpayment and the owner's intent to terminate. Paying the full amount in the manner the notice states before the three days run out bars an action for nonpayment.

A 2023 Court of Appeals decision held that an owner can't file a petition for restitution until the day after the third day. Filing on day three was premature and the petition should have been dismissed.

For other breaches, Section 47-8-33 sets a different path.

  • A first material breach calls for a written notice describing the dates and facts and saying the agreement ends in not less than seven days if the breach isn't remedied.
  • A second material breach within six months allows a notice that terminates the agreement not less than seven days after receipt.
  • The notice must be given within thirty days of the breach or of learning about it.
  • A substantial violation allows a three-day termination notice, with defenses for domestic violence victims and for residents who could not have known of or prevented the violation.
  • If a deadline to remedy lands on a weekend or federal holiday, it moves to the next business day.

Relief in court can rest only on the grounds stated in the written notice. For month-to-month tenancies, either side may end the residency with thirty days written notice before the rental date. Week-to-week residencies need seven days. If a resident holds over without consent, the owner may sue for possession, and for damages and attorney fees if the holdover is willful and not in good faith.

Retaliation

An owner can't raise rent, cut services or bring or threaten an action for possession because the resident did something protected within the previous six months. The protected acts in Section 47-8-39 include complaining to a code enforcement agency about a health and safety violation, joining a residents' association, making a written repair request, filing a fair housing complaint, testifying for another resident and abating rent as the act allows.

The protection applies to a resident who is in compliance with the rental agreement. If the owner retaliates, the resident gets the remedies in Section 47-8-48 and can raise the violation as a defense to an eviction.

There is one exception. An owner may raise rent or change services at the end of a term if the change matches what other residents of similar units receive and isn't aimed at one resident. If you plan to list a rented home, don't time a notice right after a repair complaint.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy New Mexico houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Before selling a rented house

Assume the rental agreement and the act stay in force through a sale until a lawyer tells you otherwise. The act governs how you show the house, how you handle the deposit and when you can end the tenancy.

  • Give written twenty-four hour notice for each showing, inspection or appraisal visit.
  • Keep records of rent paid, late fee notices and any repair requests.
  • Don't serve a termination or rent increase notice in a way that looks aimed at a resident who complained.
  • Decide in writing who is responsible for the deposit and the thirty-day itemization if the resident leaves around closing.
  • Check the agreement for deposit terms, because a deposit above one month's rent on an annual lease carries yearly interest.

Selling to a cash buyer can simplify some of this. Cash Home Buyers purchases houses with tenants in place and as they are, so you don't need to finish repairs or empty the unit first. Terms vary by property, and a lawyer should review the lease before you sign anything.

Frequently asked questions

How much can a New Mexico landlord charge for a security deposit?

For a rental agreement shorter than one year, no more than one month's rent. Under an annual agreement a larger deposit is allowed, but the owner must then pay the resident annual interest on it. The rule is in NMSA 47-8-18(A).

How long does a landlord have to return a deposit in New Mexico?

Thirty days from the end of the rental agreement or the resident's departure, whichever is later. If deductions are taken, the owner must send an itemized written list with the balance. Failing to do so forfeits the right to withhold and exposes the owner to court costs and attorney fees.

How much notice must a landlord give to enter a rental?

Twenty-four hours in writing, unless the owner and resident agree otherwise. The notice must state the purpose, the date and a reasonable time frame. Emergencies and repairs the resident requested within seven days are exceptions.

What is the maximum late fee in New Mexico?

Five percent of the rent for each rental period in default, and only if the rental agreement provides for a late fee. The cap was lowered from ten percent effective June 20, 2025. The owner must give notice of the fee by the end of the next rental period.

How long is the notice to leave for nonpayment of rent?

Three days after written notice of nonpayment and the owner's intent to terminate. If the resident pays everything due in the manner the notice states before the three days end, the owner can't proceed on that nonpayment.

When unpaid property tax leads to a sale

After taxes have been delinquent for three years, the state can sell the house at public auction. Section 7-38-65 NMSA 1978 allows a sale of real property for delinquent taxes at any time after three years from the first date on the delinquency list on which the taxes became delinquent. The sale has to be offered within four years of that date, with more time if a court or other legal bar gets in the way.

The debt begins well before the auction. Under 7-38-48, real property taxes are a lien on the property from January 1 of the tax year. It's a first lien that outranks every other interest, perfected or not, and it stays until taxes, penalty and interest are paid.

Interest has its own clock. Under Section 7-38-49, tax unpaid thirty days after its due date accrues interest from the thirtieth day at one percent a month or any fraction of a month. Interest is never charged on interest or on a penalty.

Since a 2013 amendment took effect on January 1, 2014, the department must offer at least one property from each county's delinquency list every year, unless the department director and the county treasurer agree in writing to postpone.

Does New Mexico sell tax liens or the property?

New Mexico sells the real property itself and then issues a deed. The Taxation and Revenue Department's Property Tax Division runs public auctions under 7-38-65, usually at the county courthouse or a similar place the department picks in the county where the property sits. There is no sale of tax lien certificates to investors.

County treasurers have a separate tool for mobile homes. Under 7-38-53, the treasurer may seize a mobile home and sell it for taxes under a demand warrant.

Sales don't happen in all 33 counties every year, and there is no fixed schedule. They are set as title research finishes and other collection efforts run out. Check the current list on the department's auction page or call the Property Tax Division at (505) 827-0883.

How the auction works

Section 7-38-67 and the department's published terms set the procedure.

  • Notice: published in a local newspaper at least once a week for the three weeks before the week of the sale, with the time, place and a property description.
  • Location: the county where the property sits, run by the department or a hired auctioneer.
  • Minimum price: no less than delinquent taxes, penalties, interest and costs combined. The department must also consider the value of the owner's interest when setting it.
  • Registration: bidders register on the day of sale. Registration begins at 8 a.m. and closes at 10 a.m. when the auction starts.
  • Bidding: oral, in person or through an agent with a notarized authorization.
  • Payment: in full by the close of the auction, by cashier's check, money order, or a personal or company check backed by a bank letter of guarantee.

A property that doesn't sell may be offered again, with the notice rules applying afresh to each sale. If it didn't bring the minimum bid, the department may re-offer it for less.

Stopping the sale

Pay everything owed, or sign an installment agreement, by 5:00 p.m. on the day before the sale. Section 7-38-65 allows either: all delinquent taxes, penalties, interest and costs paid by then, or a written installment agreement under 7-38-68 entered by then.

The installment agreement comes with limits:

  • It can't run longer than thirty-six months.
  • Interest accrues on the unpaid balance at one percent a month.
  • Signing it is an irrevocable admission of liability for the taxes covered.
  • While its terms are met, it blocks further collection action on those taxes.
  • The division may resume collection if payments are missed, other property taxes go unpaid, or another condition is broken.
  • After a breach, the original delinquency date is used to time a sale, and the division won't enter another agreement for the same taxes.
  • The division can't enter an agreement on or after the date of the initial sale.

Rights of a former owner after the sale

Former owners get no right of redemption in New Mexico, but they have two years to challenge the sale in court. That two-year window under 7-38-70 belongs to the former owner or anyone claiming through them. The only redemption period in play is the 120-day federal IRS period, which applies if the federal government holds a lien on the property.

Section 7-38-70 spells out what a challenger must prove to defeat the buyer's title. Any one of these is enough:

  • The property wasn't subject to taxation for the tax years in question.
  • The division failed to mail the required notice or to receive any required return receipt.
  • The challenger had title at the time of sale and had paid all delinquent amounts before it.
  • The challenger had an installment agreement and made every payment on time.

Courts also look hard at notice. One case found notice constitutionally inadequate when it went only to an old address after the owner had filed a change of address with the assessor. A 2024 Court of Appeals decision held that the department can invalidate a tax sale that wasn't conducted in substantial compliance with the tax code, so long as no deed has been issued. In that case the sole bidder paid the minimum price of $17,100.

What the buyer gets and what stays on the property

The buyer receives a tax deed that works like a quitclaim and carries no warranty. It conveys all of the former owner's interest as of the date the state's lien arose, subject only to perfected interests existing before that date. The sale extinguishes the tax lien only. Other liens survive, and a buyer must inspect the property and review the chain of title before bidding.

Tax sale terms for a buyer
QuestionAnswerAuthority
Which liens does the sale remove?The tax lien only; other liens are not extinguishedAuction FAQ, 7-38-67
What kind of deed?A tax deed, treated as equivalent to a quitclaim; no title warrantyAuction FAQ
When can the buyer enter?Not until the division delivers the deedAuction terms
Refund if rescinded?Only the amount paid at the sale, with no interest or buyer expensesAuction terms
Does the sale price set the new tax value?No; the county assessor determines valueAuction FAQ
Who can match the top bid?A community land grant-merced board, in limited cases inside its patent boundaries7-38-67(H)

Sales are as is, final and without refunds, and the buyer indemnifies the department for environmental conditions. Bidders can't trespass while inspecting.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy New Mexico houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Selling before the auction

An owner with equity should check this route first, because the minimum bid is set by the debt, not by the home's value. Under 7-38-67 the floor is taxes, penalties, interest and costs owed. A bidder can win at that number if nobody offers more. The department must recognize the owner's interest in any amount above the debt, but the owner has no control over how high bidding goes.

A private sale that closes before the deadline lets you set the price and the timing. The title company can pay the delinquent taxes, penalties, interest and costs from the proceeds at closing, which meets the condition in 7-38-65 if done by 5:00 p.m. the day before the auction. You need a buyer who can close quickly and take the house in its present condition.

Cash Home Buyers buys New Mexico houses as is and doesn't promise a price in advance. If your home is on a delinquency list or you've received a sale notice, tell any buyer the auction date at the start, because closing has to be scheduled around it. A tax attorney or the Property Tax Division can confirm the payoff figure.

Frequently asked questions

How long before New Mexico can sell my house for back taxes?

At least three years after the first date the taxes appear on the delinquency list. Under 7-38-65 the property must then be offered within four years of that date, unless a legal bar delays it.

Does New Mexico have a redemption period after a tax sale?

No, the state has no right of redemption for former owners. The only redemption period is the 120-day federal IRS period. Former owners have two years to challenge the sale in court under 7-38-70.

Does a tax sale wipe out my mortgage?

The sale extinguishes the tax lien only, not other liens. The deed is subject to perfected interests that existed before the property tax lien arose. Ask an attorney how that applies to your loan.

Can I make payments instead of losing the house?

Yes, through an installment agreement under 7-38-68, if signed by 5:00 p.m. the day before the sale. It runs up to thirty-six months at one percent monthly interest, and the division can't enter one on or after the initial sale date.

How much interest accrues on unpaid New Mexico property tax?

One percent a month or any fraction of a month, starting on the thirtieth day after the tax is due, under 7-38-49. No interest is charged on interest or on any penalty.
